prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest combination on this shortlist of an original idea, a decisive demonstration and broad, independently verified consequences. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the lattice-induced shift that had stood in the way of using many neutral atoms at once, and the resulting Sr and Yb clocks, with Ye's group delivering the record systematic control and the many-body clock, now reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 in laboratories worldwide. The results feed directly into tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy at the millimetre scale, dark-sector searches and the planned redefinition of the second. The credit is a natural two-person pair and the two-name configuration matches what the supplied ballot proposes. Reproduction across many groups for roughly two decades means the science is settled, so recognition is neither premature nor contested on interpretation. It is also the leading candidate in opening support (four first places, six top-three rankings), but I rest the case on the science and not on that count: this is a precision instrument in the full sense, an advance in what we can measure and how well.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap with earlier prizes. The frequency comb (2005) and the control of single trapped ions (2012) are adjacent, and optical clocks are a field with real contributions from PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN and ion-clock groups that the supplied credit leaves out; Ye in particular built much of his record on comb and cavity-stabilised laser technology that is partly prize-recognised already. A committee could reasonably argue that the lattice-clock step is an incremental, if brilliant, refinement of a recognised line rather than a new window on nature, and that its prize-worthiness is more about metrology than about discovery. The 8th place from Johansson reflects a real concern about novelty relative to earlier prizes.

responses.point: Johansson ranks optical lattice clocks only eighth and flags that the earlier prizes on frequency combs and ion control partly overlap in subject, putting circuit QED (B034) and the Cirac-Zoller theory (B023) first and second.
responses.response: I take the overlap concern seriously, but I do not think it removes the case. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool and the 2012 prize recognised single-particle quantum control in ions and cavities; neither covers the idea of trapping thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not perturb the clock transition, which is Katori's contribution and which is what produced the stability gain. On B034 I disagree with ranking it first: with four credited names and a three-person limit one of Blais or Girvin has to be dropped, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits makes me reluctant to honour the same platform so soon. I would keep B034 below B004 for those two reasons and would not treat the overlap with earlier clock-related prizes as equivalent to a duplicate award.

responses.point: Olsson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B010) first on the strength of a theory-to-experiment success that created moire materials, with MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as the decisive pair, and places lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I agree that B010 is the most conspicuous new field on the list and that the flat-band prediction followed by the 2018 observation is exactly the theory-meets-experiment arc the prize is meant for. My disagreement is about maturity: the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, and a field less than a decade old is one where several groups are still reordering who did what first (the Dean, Young and Efetov work, and the first-author contribution of Yuan Cao). Your two-name MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero version is cleaner than the supplied trio on attribution, but it leaves out Bistritzer, whose name is on the 2011 paper, so the choice is a real cost. I would keep B010 as my first alternative and would be comfortable returning to it in a later year when the interpretive questions are more settled.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy (B032) first as a clue found in nature that opens a new observational window, and acknowledges that attribution among a large collaboration's leaders is a judgment.
responses.response: I share the view that the diffuse flux and the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results open a window and that this is the discovery type the prize favours, and I ranked B032 second for that reason. I qualify it on two points. First, the source associations are still at modest significance and the origin of the diffuse flux is not understood, so the discovery is credible but still in development. Second, the credit problem is acute: the supplied trio of Karle, Halzen and Yoshida is one defensible reading of a collaboration of hundreds, and Ahrens, Kowalski, Resconi, the AMANDA founders and the Baikal and KM3NeT groups are all plausible alternatives. Your own uncertainty about allocation is the reason I rank it behind a result whose credit is unambiguous. I also flag that I am close to this field and defer to colleagues on its weight.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks lattice clocks first, then Cirac and Zoller (B023), and treats the theory-led Cirac-Zoller proposals as the blueprint for two platforms now central to quantum technology.
responses.response: I agree with you on B004 and on the pairing being fair, but I am less convinced than you are by B023 as a second choice. The 1995 ion-trap gate proposal is a theory whose experimental realisation was by Wineland, Blatt and Monroe, and Wineland was already recognised in 2012, so honouring the theorists now means rewarding the blueprint of an area whose experimental foundation has been prized. The cold-atom simulation part overlaps directly with B016, which makes the shared credit among Zoller, Cirac, Bloch and Greiner hard to separate. I keep B023 as my second alternative because the two-person credit is clean, but I would want the committee to be explicit about why theory alone is enough.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory (B027) first as the first controlled non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, mature and widely used from transition-metal oxides to iron-based superconductors.
responses.response: Your argument that DMFT is a methodological advance with three decades of validation is persuasive on maturity, and the Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt trio is as clean as any on the list. I still place it outside my preferred configuration because the case is about a computational framework whose merit rests on being a tool in a large literature, and it received no support from any member other than you in the openings. I would not call opening support merit, but that isolation tells me the committee has not yet been convinced the achievement is distinct and decisive enough for a prize this year; I would ask you to say what experimental result it explained that other approaches could not.

uncertainties: Relative weight of Katori's magic-wavelength idea versus Ye's performance and many-body results in the credit; I cannot verify the detailed priority record independently.
Whether the committee should treat the lattice clock as a distinct prize-worthy step beyond the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control recognitions, or as the culmination of that line.
Contributions from other clock groups (PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN, ion clocks) that fall outside the supplied credit and cannot be accommodated in a three-person prize.
Whether a later year, after the redefinition of the second, would be a more natural moment, although I see no scientific reason to wait.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B004 from my profile. For B032 (IceCube), B009 and others no direct collaboration is recorded, but my professional field of experimental astroparticle physics and my PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur connections place me close to neutrino and cosmic-ray astroparticle work, so I would weigh B032 with care and consider recusal from decisions on it if it became the leading option.
